metadata.title: Measuring education: Do we need a plethora of assessment studies or just a single score?
metadata.venue: International Journal of Educational Research Open

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study uses published international assessment results at the country/region level (country mean scores) from multiple ILSA programs and cycles (PISA, TIMSS, ICILS, ICCS). Because the analysis is based on aggregated country means rather than student-level microdata, the paper does not report the application of ILSA sampling weights (e.g., student design weights) or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife) that are typically required for population-representative inference from microdata. The authors also do not describe any plausible-values (PV) re-scaling or PV-combining steps, consistent with their use of already-scaled country mean scores from the ILSA reporting. Consequently, weighting and PV handling are not part of the reported analytic pipeline; the results should be interpreted as descriptive cross-assessment similarity/dissimilarity rather than as weighted estimates of student achievement distributions.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this paper are country mean scores and cross-assessment correlation structures, not student-level cognitive achievement outcomes derived from PVs. Since the analysis is conducted at the country level using published ILSA summary statistics, PV generation/combining and student-level missing-data procedures are not applicable to the reported pipeline. The paper also does not specify any missing-data strategy for country-level aggregates, so missing-data handling is not reported.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses country/region mean scores from multiple ILSA cycles: TIMSS 2019 (Mathematics and Science; Grades 4 and 8), TIMSS 1995–2019 (Grades 4 and 8 for age-cohort comparisons), PISA 2000–2018 (Reading literacy; latest reference PISA 2018), and cross-program comparisons using ICCS 2016 (Grade 8 civic knowledge) and ICILS 2018 (Grade 8 computer and information literacy). The authors state that they included all countries that participated in the selected ILSAs, but also replicated analyses using a subset of OECD countries as a robustness check. They further note that some countries/regions were included even if they did not meet sampling criteria (or nearly met them after school replacement), to avoid an overly small number of countries for comparison.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Reading literacy, finding that This paper is a cross-assessment comparability study conducted at the country/region level, using published results from multiple ILSA programs rather than training predictive models. It compares country mean scores across domains and programs—most directly TIMSS 2019 Mathematics vs TIMSS 2019 Science (Grades 4 and 8), and TIMSS 2019 Mathematics vs ICCS 2016 (Grade 8 civic knowledge), and it examines correlations across age cohorts using TIMSS Grade 4 vs Grade 8 (1995–2019). The authors report a very high correlation (r = 0.94) between TIMSS 2019 Science and Mathematics country means, while they find weaker/less consistent relationships for science across grades over time and notable divergence when comparing core domains to non-core domains (especially ICCS and ICILS). They also use multidimensional scaling (MDS) on cross-country correlation matrices to visualize clustering into OECD/PISA core domains, IEA/TIMSS domains, and a third cluster for non-core domains. Limitations include reliance on country-level aggregates (not student-level PVs), potential comparability issues (e.g., PISA linking errors pre-2012), and the fact that the paper does not provide student-level weighting or missing-data procedures. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This is not an empirical machine-learning prediction/classification study: it uses correlational analyses and multidimensional scaling on country mean scores across ILSA programs. As a result, there are no ML algorithms to extract, no PV-based student-level targets, and no student-level sample sizes or per-country n_students reported in the provided text. The absence of main_findings rows in the ML schema is therefore appropriate because the paper’s contribution is methodological/descriptive (comparability and clustering of assessment outcomes), not predictive modeling.
